title: GeoJSON Property Key Finder: Schema Census
description: List the unique property keys used across a GeoJSON file's features with the GeoJSON Property Key Finder — the schema hiding in your data. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a four-feature sample reports three keys — name on all 4 features, type on all 4, and code on just 1 — exposing the airport’s extra field the other features never got.
quick_answer: The GeoJSON Property Key Finder lists the unique property keys used across a GeoJSON file’s features — the de facto schema hiding in the data. Paste the file and read every key: the census revealing inconsistencies, undocumented fields and the shape your styling can rely on.
steps_intro: Properties are promises. List the promises actually made:

body.t: Nobody documented the file; the keys document it themselves. The finder produces the field list documentation should have shipped. Compare across files before merging them — the
Map styles filter on properties (type = ‘airport’). Knowing which keys exist — and on how many features — prevents styles that silently match nothing.
‘name’ on 400 features and ‘Name’ on 37 is one dataset with two dialects. Key censuses surface case drift, typos and half-applied schemas.
Two files merge cleanly only if their property dialects align. List both key sets first; align; then merge.

examples.label: Example · The key on one feature

body.t: A key appearing once in 10,000 features is either a jewel (the one airport’s code) or a typo (‘naem’). The finder cannot judge — it guarantees you see it, which is where judgment starts.
‘id’ on 998 of 1,000 features means two features will break every id-based join downstream. Coverage counts per key turn schema QA from archaeology into arithmetic.

popular_table.note: The finder reads keys, not values: it reports that ‘code’ exists and where, not whether the codes are valid. Value-level QA is the next gate, and it starts from this list.

faq: Does it show property values too?
The census is of keys and their coverage. Values are your data’s content; keys are its contract — this tool audits the contract.
Properties are usually flat; where a value is itself an object, its top-level key is what the census lists — nested keys belong to that value’s own story.
A key present with value null is present — and the distinction matters: null is a statement (‘known to be none’), absence is silence. The census counts statements.
A feature’s top-level ‘id’ member is not inside properties. The finder’s world is the properties object; ids get their own mention when a file uses them.
‘code’ as string on 900 features and number on 3 is a value-type inconsistency — visible when you sample values; the key census is the alarm that sends you sampling.
Can it compare two files’ keys?
Run it on each and compare the lists — the workflow is manual and quick for pairs; schema-diff tooling automates it for pipelines.
No — ‘type’, ‘coordinates’ and ‘geometry’ are structure, not properties. The census covers the properties object only, which is where data design lives.
